slides.0.title: Climate, soil and site selection
slides.0.subtitle: Same variety, different place, different style
slides.1.title: Climate types and temperature
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Maritime climate
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Small annual temperature range, rain spread through the year, a long mild season; the risks are humidity-driven disease and vintage variation (e.g. Bordeaux)
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Continental climate
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Hot summers, cold winters, a big annual range and a shorter season; the risks are spring frost and winter freeze (e.g. Burgundy, parts of Austria)
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Mediterranean climate
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Dry, hot summers and wet winters; ripening is easy and disease low, but summer water is short, so irrigation or drought-tolerant bush vines are common (e.g. Languedoc, South Africa, Chile)
slides.1.highlights.3.title: Degree days (Winkler)
slides.1.highlights.3.content: Accumulating each growing-season day’s average temperature above a 10°C base to compare heat between regions. It measures only temperature, not sunlight, diurnal range or rain, so state its limits in essays
slides.1.content: Identifying the climate type before variety and style is the shared starting point for essays and blind tasting.
slides.2.title: Geographical influences on temperature
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Altitude
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Temperature falls about 0.6°C per 100 m of altitude; high sites bring wider diurnal ranges and stronger UV and are used to keep acidity in hot regions (e.g. Argentina, Greece)
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Aspect and slope
slides.2.highlights.1.content: South-facing slopes in the northern hemisphere and north-facing in the southern get more sun; slopes drain well and let cold air flow away, reducing frost
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Water bodies and currents
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Seas, lakes and rivers moderate temperature swings; cold currents cool coasts (Humboldt, Benguela), while warm currents extend the season (Gulf Stream)
slides.2.highlights.3.title: Wind and fog
slides.2.highlights.3.content: Cool winds or sea fog cool hot regions and reduce disease (the Cape Doctor, the Mistral, Casablanca’s morning fog); strong wind can also damage shoots and flowering
slides.2.content: Latitude is only the start; altitude, aspect, water and wind decide a vineyard’s real temperature.
slides.3.title: Soil, water and terroir
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Drainage and water holding
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Gravel and sand drain well and warm up fast; clay holds water and stays cool. The ideal is mild water stress after véraison, curbing vigour so resources go to the fruit
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Fertility and vigour
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Fertile soils drive excess vigour, shaded canopies and high, dilute yields; poor soils keep vigour in check, which is why many top regions have poor soils
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Irrigation
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Dry regions use drip irrigation to control water, even regulated deficit irrigation to improve quality; many European appellations restrict irrigation in principle, and Champagne bans it outright
slides.3.highlights.3.title: How to argue about terroir
slides.3.highlights.3.content: Terroir is the sum of climate, soil, topography and human practice. Avoid the simplistic “the soil’s taste gets into the wine”; explain how soil affects water, temperature and vigour, then link to style
slides.3.content: Scoring pattern: “soil X → affects water or temperature → vigour and ripening → style”.
slides.4.componentProps.slide.title: 🧠 Knowledge check
What is the main limitation of the degree-day (Winkler) index?
A. It applies only to red wine
B. It measures only temperature, not sunlight or rain
C. It only works in the southern hemisphere
D. It uses a 0°C base
It accumulates temperature above 10°C; other factors must be considered separately.
Roughly how much does temperature fall for every 100 m of altitude?
A. 6°C
B. No change
About 0.6°C (sources vary slightly).
Which of these is a cold current that cools coastal regions?
A. Benguela
B. Agulhas
C. Kuroshio
D. Gulf Stream
Benguela and Humboldt are cold currents; the Gulf Stream, Agulhas and Kuroshio are warm.
Why do many top regions have poor soils?
A. Poor soils keep vigour in check and concentrate the fruit
B. Poor soils maximise yield
C. The law bans fertile soils
D. Poor soils need no pruning
Fertile soils tend to cause excess vigour, shading and dilution.
